macro.title: Market context
macro.subtitle: A temperature gauge, not a timing tool: an indication of how much effort finding a buy-worthy stock will take.

buffett.name: Buffett indicator
buffett.help: Total US market capitalisation divided by GDP. Buffett called 70–80% cheap; above 150% the market is expensive, and it passed 200% in 2025. It says nothing about when to act — only how hard the hunting will be.

yieldSpread.name: Yield curve (10y − 2y)
yieldSpread.help: The gap between 10-year and 2-year Treasury yields. Negative means an inverted curve. The signal here is about direction rather than level: since the 1960s the S&P 500 averaged 14.5%/year through falling-rate periods against 0.8% through rising ones.

concentration.name: Index concentration
concentration.help: One-year return of the cap-weighted S&P 500 minus the equal-weighted one. A wide positive gap means the index is being carried by its largest members. Only 28% of constituents beat the index in 2024, a record low.

sp500Pe.name: S&P 500 P/E
sp500Pe.help: Trailing price-to-earnings for the index as a whole, as a baseline to read a single company's multiple against. Taken from SPY, which tracks the index and reports one where the index itself does not.

methodology.title: Methodology
methodology.intro: How Rich Investor decides that a stock is buy-worthy, almost there, or still one to watch — and what it deliberately does not claim to know.
methodology.conditionsIntro: Every stock on your watchlist is measured against the same nine conditions, every night. Nothing is weighted, scored or averaged: a condition either holds or it does not, and the verdict is a count. A stock meeting all nine is buy-worthy; one or two short is almost there; anything further back is still watching.
methodology.fixedTitle: Why the thresholds do not move
methodology.fixedBody: The core thresholds — the P/E ceiling of 30, the PEG bands, the 50% decline from the five-year high, the $10bn floor — are fixed and cannot be edited. That is the point of a framework: a rule you relax when a stock you like fails it is not a rule. A handful of secondary thresholds the app chose for itself are editable under Account, and any figure judged against one says so on the card.
methodology.revisitBody: Fixed means the thresholds do not bend for an individual stock, not that they are true forever. They are re-checked against fresh market data periodically, and if the evidence moves, they move — visibly, and with the reasoning recorded. A number that has never been re-examined is a habit, not a method.
methodology.honestBody: The app measures what can be measured and says so when it cannot. A condition with missing data is shown grey rather than failed, a figure that could not be reconciled says why, and the qualitative judgement — whether a decline is temporary or structural — is left to you, because no screen can answer it. It is an analysis tool, not investment advice.
methodology.creditBody: The framework this app applies is drawn from “Rijke Belegger, Arme Belegger”. The implementation, the data handling and the wording throughout the app are our own; the underlying investment method is the book's.

what.title: It is a checklist, not a crystal ball
what.body:
Rich Investor does one thing: it takes every company on your watchlist and checks it against the same nine conditions, every night. Things like whether the company is profitable, whether it is growing, whether it is carrying too much debt, and whether the price has actually fallen far enough to be interesting.

Nothing is scored or weighted. A condition either holds or it does not, and what you get is a count. That is deliberately boring — the point of a checklist is that it asks the same questions of a company you have loved for years as it does of one you found this morning.

verdicts.title: Three answers, and what they actually mean
verdicts.body:
**Buy-worthy** means all nine conditions hold. It is not an instruction to buy. It means the company has cleared every measurable bar, and the part that is left is the part only you can do.

**Almost there** means it is one or two conditions short. These are usually the interesting ones — worth knowing which condition is missing, because a company missing only the price condition is a different proposition from one missing the debt condition.

**Watching** means it is further back than that. Most companies sit here most of the time, and that is normal rather than a failure.

priceAndGrowth.title: Why the price and the growth are judged together
priceAndGrowth.body:
Two of the nine conditions do the most work, and they only make sense as a pair.

The first asks whether the price has fallen a long way from its own five-year high. A big fall is what creates the opportunity — but on its own it tells you nothing, because the most common reason a share price falls a long way is that the company genuinely got worse.

The second, the PEG ratio, asks whether you are paying a sensible price for the growth you are actually getting. A cheap share in a company that is not growing is not cheap, it is just cheap-looking.

A fall tells you something *might* be on offer. The growth test tells you whether it is a good company that got cheap, or simply a bad one. Neither question is worth much without the other.

yours.title: The last step is yours
yours.body:
The app measures what can be measured and stops there. It will not tell you whether a company's problem is a bad quarter or the beginning of the end, because no screen can answer that.

So every stock has a qualitative review: a short set of questions about whether the trouble looks temporary or structural, what might turn it around, and what would make you sell. Answer them in your own words. That is the judgement the numbers are there to inform, not replace.

This is an analysis tool, not investment advice.
